title: a test that pipes into grep -q no longer fails at random, and the lint that forbids it covers the test suites
acceptance: On T-088's head, tests/adapter-contract.test.sh failed twice in CI with a different 'missing' signature each time ([status 429] [network error while], then [expired api key]), yet passed locally on main and on the branch. The cause is its completeness loop, `printf '%s\n' "$broken_lines" | grep -qiE "$alt" || unread=...`, under `set -o pipefail`. grep -q exits on its first match, printf can then die of SIGPIPE, the pipeline returns 141, and a signature that does match gets reported as unread, at random. bin/ci.sh already forbids `| grep -q` and `| grep -c` for exactly this reason, but its lint only scans bin/*.sh and bin/adapters/*.sh, so the test suites slipped through. Commit the task's own entry as design/tasks/T-103.json on this branch. Evidence is the required GitHub check and the seven gates.

Fix the adapter-contract loop with a here-string, e.g. `grep -qiE "$alt" <<<"$broken_lines"`. Then sweep every test suite (tests/*.sh and below) for the same construct (a pipeline into grep -q or grep -c) and fix each one the same way. Report the sweep in a SWEPT: line listing the files and the count.

Extend bin/ci.sh's lint to scan the test suites too, keeping its comment filter and its fm:lint-source marker rule, so the construct cannot come back. The lint fails on a suite that reintroduces it: add a fixture or self-test that proves this, and it fails on the current code.

A deterministic test shows the old construct could misreport. Force the SIGPIPE path, for example by piping a large input through a producer that keeps writing after grep -q has matched, and show the here-string form never misreports.
Stay inside this scope. If the work needs a file outside it, stop and name the file and the reason.
